titolo: How Ordinary Families Made a Dollar Last a Week During the Great Depression

scene.testo: Millions of families lived on almost nothing, and survived.
Nothing was wasted. Not bread, not string, not fabric.
Flour sacks became dresses, curtains, and children's shirts.
Stale bread turned into pudding or breadcrumbs.
Worn-out socks were darned again and again.
By 1933, about one in four workers had no job.
Wages were cut, hours were cut, and savings vanished.
So the kitchen became the center of the household economy.
Families planted gardens in every yard they had.
Mothers canned vegetables to last through the winter.
Worn collars were flipped and sewn back on.
Neighbors traded eggs, labor, and vegetables instead of cash.
Many meals were built around beans, potatoes, and cornbread.
But the smartest trick wasn't about food at all.
It was a habit nearly every household shared.
It cost nothing, yet it stretched every paycheck further.
Stay with me, and I'll show you.
